intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that monilethrix-2 (MNLIX2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the type II hair cortex keratin gene hHb1 (HHB1).

checks.claim: Monilethrix-2 (MNLIX2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the type II hair cortex keratin gene hHb1 (HHB1).
checks.evidence_quote: In the second family, we identified in affected individuals a lysine substitution of the corresponding glutamic acid residue, Glu 403, in the type II hair keratin hHb1
checks.explanation: The abstract supports causation by an hHb1 mutation in a monilethrix family, but it does not say outright that the hHb1 mutation is heterozygous (only the hHb6 mutations are called heterozygous). The 'monilethrix-2' designation is not in the paper.

paragraphs.text: Monilethrix-2 is an inherited hair disorder characterized by beaded (moniliform) hair. Its severity can vary widely within one family, from dystrophic alopecia with follicular keratosis to moniliform hair that can be seen only by electron microscopy (Winter et al., 1998).

checks.evidence_quote: Monilethrix is a rare dominant hair disease characterized by beaded or moniliform hair which results from the periodic thinning of the hair shaft
checks.explanation: The disease is described as beaded/moniliform hair.

checks.claim: The severity of monilethrix-2 can vary widely within one family, from dystrophic alopecia with follicular keratosis to moniliform hair visible only by electron microscopy.
checks.evidence_quote: one with pronounced dystrophic alopecia, follicular keratosis, and clear-cut moniliform hair, and one with no hair loss at all and moniliform hair detectable only by electron microscopy
checks.explanation: The two infants in one family show this range of severity.

paragraphs.text: Winter et al. (1998) reported a French monilethrix family with a particularly variable phenotype. The pedigree included 2 infants. One had pronounced dystrophic alopecia, follicular keratosis and clear-cut moniliform hair. The other had no hair loss at all, and the moniliform hair could be detected only by electron microscopy. An adult family member had no clinical or electron microscopic signs of the disorder but had clear historical proof of the disease.

paragraphs.text: In affected individuals from a monilethrix family, Winter et al. (1997) identified a glu403-to-lys (E403K) substitution in the type II hair keratin hHb1. This glutamic acid residue corresponds to glu410 in hHb6, which lies in the helix termination motif. Because the hHb6 E410K mutation had been found in other monilethrix patients, the authors suggested that this site is a mutational hotspot in these closely related type II hair keratins.

paragraphs.text: Winter et al. (1998) noted that the monilethrix mutations reported so far in the type II hair cortex keratins hHb6 and hHb1 were restricted to glu413 (glu117 of the 2B subdomain) of the helix termination motif. In a French monilethrix family, they identified a new lysine substitution of another highly conserved glutamic acid residue in hHb1. This change, glu402-to-lys (E402K), affects glu106 of the 2B subdomain in the EIATYRRLLEGEE motif. It was present in 2 infants, one severely and one mildly affected, and in an adult with a history of the disease but no current symptoms.

paragraphs.text: In a French family with monilethrix (MNLIX2), Winter et al. (1998) identified a glu402-to-lys (E402K) substitution in hHb1. The mutation affects a highly conserved glutamic acid residue (glu106 of the 2B subdomain) in the EIATYRRLLEGEE helix termination motif. Family members carrying it had a particularly variable phenotype. One infant had pronounced dystrophic alopecia, follicular keratosis and clear-cut moniliform hair. A second infant had no hair loss and moniliform hair detectable only by electron microscopy. An adult had no clinical or electron microscopic signs but had clear historical proof of the disease.
